THE EUROPEAN WAR CLOUD
PASSED AWAY.
The war cloud that menaced, fora while,
the peace of Western Europe has passed by
and left the sky serene once more. This
happy result is credited by the leading Eng
lish journals to the recent visit of the Em
peror of All the Russias and his chief ad-
viser. Prince Gortsehakoff, to the German
capital, where their presence allayed-how
we are not privileged to know—the war fever
that threatened to become epidemic. The
rumor that the Cabinet at Berlin—or perhaps
it would be more correct to say, Prince Bis
marck —had forwarded a note to the French
Government at Paris, complaining of arma-
ments in France and demanding that they be
discontinued, turns out to have been un
founded; and when Sir Charles Dilke re
cently asked Mr. Robert Bourke, Under-
Secretary for Foreign Affairs, if there was
any truth in the report, he was informed, in
reply, that " there was now no further cause
‘* for apprehension that the peace of Europe
" is likely to be disturbed." That Germany
—although German journals have, since the
war which contributed so much to the glory
and the prestige of their country,
shown a disposition to indulge, some
what too freely, in the gasconade that
once characterized their neighbors—has
experienced an uneasy feeling for some time
back, has been evident. Several causes may
be assigned for this—some internal, others
external. Of the first class the religious
question is much the most serious. In
German Poland, in Bavaria, indeed in near-
ly all South Germany, and in the Rhine
Provinces, there is a large, perhaps a pre
dominant,Catholic population ; and while the
records of the late war show that they fought
not less bravely than their Protestant fellow-
countrymen of the North for home and
Fatherland, they can hardly help feeling that
the man of “ blood and iron” has laid a
heavy hand upon their creed and its most il-
lustrious professors. It would seem that
Prince Bismarck is pursuing in Southern
Germany the same policy that Wentworth,
Earl of Strafford, pursued in Ireland, which
Laud so much admired—albeit, a minister of
the Gospel of Peace—and which, under its
name of " Thorough," may reckon among its
admirers to-day both James Anthony Froude
and Thomas Carlyle. The fate of Went-
worth is known and the result of
his policy ; those of his distinguished
imitator - have yet to be determined.
Where a Government is forced to resort to
fines, to confiscations, to imprisonment and
to banishment in this age of boasted civil
and religious freedom, to compel obedience
to its authority, it must needs have grave
reasons for apprehension of the external
causes for uneasiness. France, though not
the only one, is undoubtedly the most promi-
nent. At the outset of the late Franco-
Prussian War the opinion and the sympathy
of Europe and America generally were in
favor of Germany, but as the struggle pro
gressed the tide turned in favor of the unfor
tunate France. The marvelous successes of
the German Arms filled men with admiration,
not unmingled with dismay, while the utter
prostration of France excited pity. When
the war ended, if the victors had been con
tent with the full payment of its expenses by
the vanquished, had taken the amplest securi
ties. for future peace, had insisted upon the
fortresses of Metz and Strasburg being razed
to the ground, the world would have ap
plauded German generosity as it applauded
German bravery. But a sterner and
more vigorous policy unhappily pre
vailed. The indemnity imposed on the
conquered country was enormous and un-
paralleled, and to ensure its payment por
tions of the German • army remained as an
army of occupation. But to humble the
French still more, and to keep the feud be-
tween the two countries still alive, two pro
vinces were wrested from their country and
annexed to Germany. There is no doubt
Prince Bismarck had miscalculated the recu
perative energy of France and the extent of
her resources. He probably fancied that the
hard conditions he imposed would have the
effect of crippling her for years to come.
His disappointment must, therefore, have
been great when his mistake was clearly
proven. The war indemnity of France, enor
mous as it was, has been paid with signal
demonstration of her large internal resources
—the re-organization of her army has been
very considerably advanced, and, at the same
time, the feeling of angry apprehension in
Germany has become greatly intensified.
It is feared, and not without cause, that
France will spring at the throat of Ger-
many the first favorable opportunity that
offers. No doubt of it. Frenchmen are
but mortals, as Germans are, and
cannot, if they would, forget what they have
endured. But if the reports of a week or two
ago might be credited, it was the intention
of Germany to render such a chance
impossible. However, the leading men in
the military and political German world hold
and declare the opinion that France, under
whatever changes of Government, cherishes
the fixed intention of a war of revenge, and
,moves steadily and rapidly towards it. They
find in the proportions of the army which
France is reconstructing, and in the burdens
which are silently incurred for its develop
ment, proof positive that she will not accept,
even temporarily,less than her old position as
a dominant Power on the Continent, and
that she views the recovery of Alsace and
Lorraine as the indispensable step for regain
ing her inf uence. This being the case, they
ask each other whether it is right or wrong,
sensible or suicidal, to wait, the strength of
Germany being now at its greatest, until
France has gathered up her utmost aggressive
forces, and completed her immense defensive
schemes. Had the opinions of these men
prevailed, we make little doubt war would
have been precipitated ere this.. But the
Court and people of Germany are averse to it,
and neighboring powers will not suffer it.
The Czar, Alexander II., is said to be
an amiable man, much more inclined
to the arts of peace than to sangui
nary strife. Although on friendly terms
with the Hohenzollerns, he is the Em
peror of Russia, and the leading men of his
Court and country are opposed to any further
aggrandizement of Germany. Circumstances
are such now in Europe that Alexander II. is
really the arbiter of peace and war, and peace
happens to be, at present, for the interests of
Russia. We may, therefore, safely calculate on
it until fresh complications arise to disturb it.
France is silently progressing in her work. A
notable change has come over her press, her
people and her politicians. The strife of
parties has, for the time, apparently ceased.
Imperialist, Orleanist, Legitimist and Repub
lican have sunk, in their country's behalf,
partyism in patriotism. The whole people
seem to have grown soberer, and to have ex
changed their proverbial volatility for the
sedateness of the Teutonic races. How true
it is that misfortune and suffering purify a
people. The prudence of the French rulers
and public men, the circumspection of the
French press and the good sense of the French
people will not, it may be hazarded, afford
soon any sufficient casus belli to the Berlin
war party. The next European struggle will,
in all likelihood, be a religious one, the end of
which no one can tell.

ber, had any direct concern. Of course it

chise for election to the House of Commons,

gested that the basis of the franchise

ercise of the franchise various classes of the

educator in the duties of citizenship, and the

rapidly would they permeate the community
with the feelings of citizenship, with the de
sire to deal with political issues and grapple

to the education of a free people. He
should not do more than touch on the ques
tion of the simplification of the laws relating

this direction by Mr. Mowat, but more might
be done, and a glorious work remained for

dealings between man and man. He had no
doubt that they would find this matter pro
perly dealt with in the Local Legislature

canvassers in elections, who, with an ardour

ting voters to the poll, got fatigued with the
operation, and thought a better plan than

poll could be adopted, and a remedy found,
he had no doubt that the remedy would be
applied. His opinion was that it was their
duty to go to the polls, and that it was the
duty of the Legislature to place upon the
statute books a law inculcating that duty.
The result of telling the people," This is
your duty, do it ; you must "—would be to

better, and more unbiassed expression of
public opinion. (Cheers.) He had no doubt

one who neglected to exercise the franchise

the fullest vote they had ever seen, which
they would agree would be conducive, to a
good election to his friends who some time

said that he believed our present system of

He intended to make it his business on an

this object; and although he could not hope

Yesterday at 2 p.m. the Returning-officer
for South Bruce, no opposition having been
offered, declared Hon. Edward Blake, Q.C.,
re-elected by acclamation. The occasion of
his going back to his constituents was
brought about by his acceptance of a Govern
ment position, with emolument, as Minister
of Justice. Mr. Blake was in Walkerton, but
did not intend to address the electors at all,
as he had presumed the quiet and even un
interesting proceedings of a nomination,
under the Dominion Election Act, would not at
tract any large number of the people. In this
he was mistaken, for there was a very large
attendance of the electors together with
political leaders, who were anxious to hear
the distinguished hon. gentleman deliver his
views upon the leading questions of the day.
Mr. Blake gratified them to some extent, in
that he made an impromptu speech, in which
he referred to several matters, now more or
less engrossing public attention.
The organs have manifestly been very de
sirous of having Mr. Blake explain how it was
that he " captured ?” Mr. Mackenzie, or how
the latter " captured” him. Knowing as they
do that he is a profound thinker and that,
after he has reached a certain point in weigh
ing and testing the questions of the day, he
has no uncertain opinion on them and is not
afraid to express it, they had hoped that
either the Administration had compelled him
to recede from certain advanced opinions, or
that he had succeeded in bringing it up to his
own standpoint. Either of these situations,
if so confessed by him, would, of course,
afford a handsome text for their re
marks, a good subject for their auguries,
or a horoscope by which they might, with
their usual exactitude, read the future and
predict coming events. They have been
disappointed. It is true that Mr. Blake still
holds to the utterances which have marked
the man as an original thinker, and he offers
his reason which cannot very well be quar-
relled with. He thinks that instead of
blaming a man for enquiring into political
issues and endeavoring to alter and improve
them by new treatment, instead of abusing a
person who starts subjects for thought and
seeks new stand points from which the pub-
lic should impartially and calmly view
them, that he should be praised. That
man, who enlarges the horizon of his own
and his neighbor's vision is a more valua
ble member of the community than one
who either contracts the range or refuses to
use new points. Though it may be esteemed
by the people as unpopular and unnecessary,
a fresh idea or notion should be received
with attention and not condemnation. The
mere enunciation or promulgation of an
opinion does not necessarily create it
a component part of fixed public
doctrine or faith. If it bear fair
criticism and testing, its value will be
shown thereby, but the same means are
equally potent to point out its weakness and
worthlessness, if such components it contain.
It was in this spirit of starting public
thought that Mr. Blake gave to the world his
opinions, in years gone by, on certain politi
cal questions. They had been carefully pre
pared and elaborated, and if he deemed
them fit to publish he was but exercising the
right of a British subject in using his privi-
leges of free speech and writing, which he
claims to find are used with‘less freedom
** in democratic Canada than in aristocratic
" England."
The Minister of Justice told his hearers
that he and the Government are in perfect
accord. In one matter—the Esquimault and
Nanaimo Railway, they had differed some
what, but before he assumed office he and
they, by means of conferences, had arrived
at a satisfactory basis for the readjustment of
this question, a basis he was not at liberty
to refer to, as final negotiations were still un
concluded, but he was confident that, at the
proper time and place, such a policy would be
brought down on this question as would be
satisfactory to the people as it was already to
himself. He expressed his gratification with
the financial policy of the Administration
and referred warmly to the best loan yet
"placed" on the British market, as having
been secured by Mr. Cartwright. The Elec
tion Act, the Insolvency Law, the Supreme
Court Bill, the Senate Resolutions, our rela-
tions with the mother country, and other
subjects were touched upon. Several of these
were measures the preceding Government
were unable to create law, but they had been
triumphantly mastered by the Reform Ad
ministration.
In the brief space at our disposal to-day, we
can give little else than an outline of the
Minister's speech, the one half of which ap
pears in this issue. As has ever been the
case since Mr. Blake entered public life,

VERDICT OF MANSLAUGHTER,
The inquisition relating to the death of the
late G. B. C. McAndrew, in Toronto, was
pleted yesterday evening before Coroner
Riddel.
The Coroner having opened the Court,
asked the prisoners if they had any state
ments to make, and said they had liberty to
do so if they wished. He observed that if
they said anything which would criminate
themselves it might and could be used here
after against them.
John Ray said he did not see McAndrew
at all.
Thomas Kenny did not see the deceased in
front of the house.
William Costigan and John Reehill never
saw the man and knew nothing of the affair.
Thomas Duffy did not see the man, and
was not within ten yards of the house at the
time. -
The Coroner then read over to the jury the
chief points in the evidence, and delivered
his charge, in which he confined the crime,
if the prisoners were found guilty, to man-
slaughter.
The jury retired, and having deliberated
for nearly two hours, returned the following
verdict: "That the said George B. C. Mc
Andrew came to his death from apoplexy, in-
duced by excitement, caused by the disturb-
ance at his house on the 25th of May last,
and we find a verdict of manslaughter against
John Ray, William Costigan, Thomas Kenny
and Thomas Duffy."
The Coroner committed the prisoners for
trial.
PACKAGES FORWARDED EIGHT MILES IN Two
SECONDS.—On Sunday, Feb. 28, the pneuma-
tic mail system was opened for public use in
the city of Vienna, and for a few days of its
working it appears to have been eminently
satisfactory. By this method letters and pack-
ages not exceeding two ounces in weight can
be sent from one end of the city to another—a
distance of about eight miles—in something
less than two seconds, so that, adding to this
the time necessary for making up packages,
assorting them, and delivering them, the
whole is just about one hour. But this
only covers extreme distances, and the
managers of this system in Vienna say
that in a short time the time between the re-
ceipt and delivery will be greatly reduced. In
fact, between stations only two or three miles
distant from each other, such packages are
even now delivered within twenty minutes
after being deposited. As the General Post-
office in Vienna is also in the building of the
general telegraph office, powerful steam en
gines are constantly at work compressing at
mospheric air in a mammoth reservoir, from
which the double system of cast-iron pipes,
laid three feet under the surface of the
streets is fed. One system of pipes
serves for carrying packages, and the other
for pushing them ahead in the other di-
rection. At the seven principal stations, in
various parts of the city, similar engines are
kept at work day and night drawing the air
from the pipes and creating a vacuum in front
of the packages, which are thus more readily
pressed forward by the expansive force of the
compressed air behind them. The 60 sub-
stations are connected not only with the two
central offices, but also with each other by
this double system of pipes. The despatch
of each package is announced by telegraph to
the office to which it is sent, and to all inter
vening offices, to advise the latter not to stop
it on its way. The pipes are six inches in
diameter, with a perfectly smooth, polished
inner surface, and the packages are made up
in india-rubber cylinders of various lengths.
The postage on mail matter must be prepaid
at the rate of two kreutzers (one cent) for
each half half ounce or fraction, which is
evidently much cheaper than the two cent
postage for the city letters in this country.
This is the first instance of a large city—
Vienna has about 900,000 inhabitants—giving
its people such facilities of correspondence at
a moderate cost.—N. Y. Mercury.

PAINFUL ACCIDENT.
A Man has the Calf of his Leg almost
-torn away.
On Wednesday last an accident of an ex-
ceedingly painful and dangerous nature oc-
curred to a man named Dan Overton, who is em-
ployed in casting at Laidlaw’s Foundry, on the
corner of Mary and Kelly streets. It appears
that Overton was engaged with another man
in removing a large casting from the furnace,
on which some fins were remaining, which on
turning the casting round caught the trousers
and calf of Overton's leg, tearing nearly the
whole of the fleshy part of the leg off. The
pain was intense as the fins were red hot, and
burnt as well as tore the flesh. The sufferer
was sent away immediately in a cab to Dr.
Mullin’s, and is, we believe, progressing favor
ably.

A TRUANT PROTEGE. —The London Daily
Standard, of May 15, has the following: A
romantic affair has just happened at Liver
pool. A young lady, who had been brought
up by a clergyman's wife at a rectory near
Chester, a week or two ago contrived, by an
ingenious pretence, to obtain a considerable
sum of money from the lady, together
with permission to go to the city,
and having reached Chester she was privately
married, by license, to a person who, a few
days afterwards, sailed for America, leaving
numerous creditors-betting and otherwise.
A few days ago she disappeared from the rec
tory, leaving a farewell note that she intended
to join her husband. The Police in Liverpool
were communicated with, and the clergyman's
wife proceeded to that town at the earliest
possible moment in the hope of intercepting
the fugitive. She arrived at the landing stage
on Thursday, just in time to find her protege
on board the tender of the White Star steamer
Britannic, and on the point of sailing for
New York. A scene of a highly dramatic
nature followed. The excited lady
rushed on the lender and forcibly
dragged the girl to the stage, uttering dis
jointed and hysterical exclamations, and when
both were on terrq firma she broke out into a
torrent of reproaches which caused the fair
defaulter to sob loudly, and attracted a large
number of spectators, At length some de-
gree of calmness was restored, and the party
drove to a hotel, the services of the police
officer who had been in attendance to take
the runaway into custody if necessary being
unrequired, The young lady was accom
panied by her maid.

THE RECOVERY OF SUNKEN TREASURE.—The
steamship Dido, belonging to the London and
Edinburgh Shipping Company, left Leith for
Vigo on May 11, with a number of divers on
board. The vessel has been chartered by a
London salvage company for the purpose of .
carrying on operations to recover treasure
sunk in the harbor at Vigo in the form of
specie and plate valued at several millions.
The treasure was lost in 1702, when a rich
fleet of Spanish galleons, with a convoy of
French ships of the line, were attacked by the
combined English and Dutch fleets in Vigo
harbor. The French were beaten, and the
galleons fell into the hands of the conquerors,
with the exception of six, which were set on
fire and sunk by the Spaniards to save them
from being captured. More than one at
tempt has already been made to recover the
treasure, but these have failed from the want,
it is stated, of proper appliances. In the
event of the treasure being recovered a
royalty of forty-three and a half per cent will
be paid to the Spanish Government.

FIRE AT JanVIS.—Yesterday afternoon be
tween 2 and 3 p. m. a fire broke out in the
plaining mill and sash, blind and door fac
tory belonging to Mr. Whitside, of Delhi, and
which was managed by Mr. Healey. The
cause of the fire was the upsetting of a lamp,
which was used to boil glue: Two men on
the spot tried to extinguish the flames, but
owing to so many shavings being about, were
unable to do so. The mill was entirely de
stroyed, as was all the carpenter's tools, the
books, about 10,000 feet of lumber, and 150
doors all ready made. The building and
machinery, owned by Mr. Whitside, is insur-
ed for $2,000, but the loss to him will be be
tween $3,000 and $4,000. Mr. Healey, who
own's all the material and the lumber, is un
insured, and he estimates his loss at between
$2,000 and $3,000. The carpenters lose be
tween $50 and $100 worth of tools.
JUNE.—Ovid, in his Fasti, makes Juno
claim the honor of giving a name to this
month ; but there had been ample time be
fore his day for an obscurity to invest the
origin of the term, and he lived before it was
the custom to investigate such matters criti
cally. Standing as the fourth month in the
Roman calendar, it was in reality dedicated
a Jumoribus—that is, to the junior or infe-
rior branch of the original legislature of
Rome, as May was a majoribus, or to the
supreme branch. Romulus assigned to this
month a complement of thirty days, though
in the old Latin or Alban calendar, it con
sisted of twenty-six only. Numa deprived it
of one day, which was restored by Julius
Cæsar ; since which time it has remained un-
disturbed.
